title: Understanding AMH: What Your Egg Reserve Test Means
author: Dr. Ananya Mehta
excerpt: AMH is one of the most talked-about fertility tests. Here is what it tells you — and what it does not.
content: Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH) is produced by small follicles in the ovaries. A simple blood test gives an estimate of how many eggs remain, often called your ovarian reserve.

AMH helps your doctor plan the right medication dose for IVF and predict how the ovaries may respond. It is a helpful planning tool, but it does not measure egg quality and cannot on its own predict whether you will conceive naturally.

A low AMH is not a reason to panic. Many women with low AMH conceive, with or without treatment. The best next step is to discuss your result together with your age, ultrasound findings and medical history.
If you are thinking about delaying pregnancy, checking AMH can help you decide whether egg freezing is worth considering.

title: Your IVF Journey, Step by Step
author: Dr. Rohan Desai
excerpt: From the first injection to the pregnancy test — a calm, clear walkthrough of an IVF cycle.
content: Every IVF cycle begins with a plan made for you. After baseline tests, you start daily hormone injections that help several eggs mature at the same time.
During the next 10–12 days we monitor your follicles with ultrasound and blood tests. When they are ready, a trigger injection prepares the eggs for collection.
Egg retrieval is a short procedure under anaesthesia. The same day, eggs are fertilised in the lab using conventional IVF or ICSI, and embryos are cultured for 3–5 days.
One healthy embryo is gently transferred into the uterus, and good-quality extra embryos can be frozen for the future. About two weeks later, a blood test confirms whether you are pregnant.

title: 5 Lifestyle Changes That Support Male Fertility
author: Dr. Neel Patel
excerpt: Sperm take around three months to develop, so small changes today can make a real difference.
content: Stop smoking and limit alcohol. Both are linked to lower sperm count and movement.
Keep a healthy weight and stay active. Regular moderate exercise helps hormone balance, while very intense training without rest can have the opposite effect.
Avoid excess heat — long hot baths, saunas and laptops on the lap can raise testicular temperature.
Eat a balanced diet rich in fruit, vegetables, nuts and whole grains, and speak to your doctor before taking supplements.
Manage stress and sleep well. Because sperm take about 70–90 days to mature, give any change at least three months before repeating a semen analysis.

title: Coping With the Emotional Side of Fertility Treatment
author: MOMFertility Counselling Team
excerpt: Hope, worry and waiting are all part of the journey. Practical ways to look after yourselves.
content: It is completely normal to feel anxious, sad or overwhelmed during treatment. Naming these feelings is the first step to managing them.
Talk openly with your partner and agree on how much you want to share with family and friends. Protecting your energy is not selfish.
Simple routines help: short walks, regular sleep, and breathing exercises during the two-week wait.
Professional counselling is a sign of strength, not weakness. Our counsellors are here for you before, during and after every cycle.
